How she works

You bring the complaint. She brings the method.

A conversation, not a dashboard
YouInvoices go out late and I chase them myself. KORATwo separate things are happening: invoices are written days after the job closes, and nobody follows up before day thirty. Which one first?
KORAYou have sent forty‑one of these quotes. Thirty‑eight use the same six fields. Let me read the last three before I call it a rule.
KORAChecked. Written down as quote_standard_v3: job sheet, your margin, the PDF, the draft email. YouDo it.
YouWhat margin did we agree here? KORAEighteen percent. You approved it on 14 March, in Dana’s notes. Dana left in June; the rule stayed.
YouCan you file our sales tax? KORANo. I can prepare the numbers. I will not say I can file it until that is true.

You describe what annoys you, in your words. I work out what is actually broken underneath it — usually more than one thing.

Before I propose anything I look at how the work really runs today, not how it is supposed to run. Guessing here is how AI gets your details wrong.

Once something has been done right and you have agreed with it, it stops being a conversation and becomes how the business does that job.

Every answer traces back to a decision, a document or a date you can open. Nothing arrives with no history behind it.

You decide what I may do alone and where I must stop and ask. Being able to reach something is not permission to act on it.

KORALook at the last one again. I would rather tell you I cannot do something than promise it and be wrong. That is not modesty — it is the only way an owner can safely stop checking my work.

Why a box at all

Not every task deserves a premium AI bill.

No AI where plain software is enough.

Most operating work is not a thinking problem. Moving something, checking a field, formatting a document, sending the reminder on day seven — ordinary software has done that for thirty years, and it costs nothing per use.

Cheapest · most of the day
Local AI when local is enough.

The Core arrives with its own on‑board AI capability. Reading, sorting, drafting and all the ordinary understanding work can happen on hardware the business has already paid for — without a meter running.

Already paid for · runs on your Core
Frontier AI when the judgment is worth paying for.

When a decision genuinely needs the strongest model available, KORA reaches for it. That is exactly where the money should go — and nowhere else.

Paid per use · on purpose

We do not publish a savings percentage, because we cannot know your workload before we see it. What we publish is the rule KORA works by — and you can hold her to it.

You already have years of business history.

Contracts, emails, quotes, spreadsheets, projects, the rules nobody wrote down. Getting an AI to know all of that is real work in itself. Why should premium AI have to read every routine file at premium prices? The Core does the long, ordinary part of getting to know your company at home — and saves the expensive intelligence for the part that actually needs it.

The Core is compute you already own

Your team goes home.
KORA can keep working.

Evenings, nights and weekends, the machine in your office is sitting there already paid for. The heavy, patient, unglamorous jobs — reading a year of files, tidying a client history, preparing a long report — do not need anyone watching them happen.

Give KORA the big job before you leave.

Your AI can change.
What she knows about your business stays.

Models will keep getting better and keep getting replaced. That is fine — and it is exactly why what your company teaches her should not live inside one supplier’s account.

The intelligence underneath can be swapped as the market moves. What was learned about your business is kept with your business.

KORAAsk the question the other way round, because it is the one that matters.

Everything you have approved keeps running on your own Core. That is the difference between a tool you rent and a system that belongs to the company.

How to judge what she is worth

Saving you hours is the small half.
The other half is money.

Most of what a business loses is not wasted spending. It is money already earned that quietly leaves, and money sitting inside the company that nobody went and collected. KORA is built to count those separately — and to show her working.

How KORA counts. Three numbers, each traced to a real event.

Example figures · not a client result
Generated $6,800

New money that exists because the work actually got done.

  • A lead answered in minutes instead of days
  • Past clients who were due the same service again
  • A second service the client already needed
Recovered $4,200

Money already earned that was on its way out of the door.

  • An invoice past due, chased and paid
  • A contract about to lapse, renewed in time
  • A quote nobody had answered, reopened
Saved $1,700

Money the business did not spend that it was about to.

  • Two overlapping tools, one cancelled
  • Work drafted here instead of bought outside
  • An auto‑renew stopped before it billed

Each line traces back to one event, with a date and a source you can open.

Three numbers, never one. KORA will not blend them into a single flattering ROI figure. Money saved is not the same thing as money earned, and an owner deserves to see which is which.

Only what she can prove. No estimated hours, no assumed value, no “probably would have”. If KORA cannot show you the event behind a number, the number does not get counted — and she will tell you that too.

Straight answers

The six things owners actually ask.

Is this just a chatbot with a box around it?

No. A chatbot answers a question and forgets you. KORA keeps the approved context of one specific business — what was decided, what is happening now, and what she is allowed to do — and carries operating work forward inside those limits.

Talking is how you reach her. It is not what she is.

What exactly am I paying $300 a month for?

For KORA working, not for permission to use software. It covers her configuration for how your business actually runs, keeping her current, the routing that decides what runs on your own Core and what does not, new rules and workflows as you ask for them, and a team behind her when something needs a person.

Paid yearly it is $2,400 — $200 a month. Month to month it is $300, and you can stop whenever you like.

Where does my business data actually live?

The Core sits in your business, and the ordinary day‑to‑day work happens on it. We do not claim that nothing ever leaves — that would not be true of any capable system, and we would rather be straight with you.

When a task genuinely needs the strongest outside model, KORA uses one, and you set the rules for what may go out and what may not. Access is not authority: being able to see something is not the same as being allowed to act on it.

What happens if I stop paying?

The Core stays yours. Your data stays yours. Everything KORA already built for the business stays. It was bought, not licensed.

What stops is the service around her: configuration, routing, updates, hosted infrastructure and support.

When does the subscription actually start?

After your Core is delivered and activated — not when it ships. Days spent in a courier van are never days you paid for.

What if we grow and outgrow the one we bought?

You upgrade the Core, you do not replace it. Memory and storage go up inside the same machine. Growing a business should not mean buying the whole thing again.

People are added separately: $600 a year each, or $99 a month.

Some people want to build a corporation. Others don’t, and we want them to have that choice.
